, and page 1 is instant. Then a partner's nightly sync starts walking every page, and each request is slower than the last. In a test on SQL Server 2022 with 1,000,000 orders and an index matching the sort, page 1 read 4 pages. Page 10,000 read 958, and the last page, 50,000, read 4,702: every entry of the index, to return 20 rows. The version that selected every column read 613,467 pages for page 10,000, more than twelve times the size of the whole table. The keyset version read 6 pages, whichever page it fetched.
jumps to row 19,981, so page 1,000 costs the same as page 1.

It reads like an address, and arrays have taught everyone that indexing by position is free. Tests run on page 1, development databases have a few hundred rows, and the plan doesn't warn you: with a good index, page 1 and page 50,000 get the same Index Scan under the same Top operator. Only the actual row counts differ, and nobody looks at those on a query that was fast yesterday.
An index finds values, not positions

A B-tree can go straight to "the first order before 10:42 on March 3" in a few reads, because that's a value it stores. "The 19,981st order" isn't stored anywhere. As Use The Index, Luke puts it, the database must count all rows from the beginning until it reaches the requested page. PostgreSQL's docs say the same: the rows skipped by an
clause still have to be computed inside the server, so a large
might be inefficient. In the test's actual plans, the Index Scan under the Top returned 20,000 rows for page 1,000 and 1,000,000 rows for the last page.
Skipping happens at the very end, after everything below it in the plan has run. In the test,
used the same index plus a

for the other columns, and the Top sat above the lookups. So page 1,000 looked up 20,000 rows to return 20, and read 61,376 pages; page 10,000 read 613,467. Any join, function or lookup in the query runs for the rows you throw away, too.
Pages drift when the data changes
Each page is a separate query, so

means "skip whatever the first 20 rows are now." In the test, three new orders arrived after page 1 was read, and page 2 began with the last three orders of page 1. Deletes do the opposite and skip rows. Microsoft's
docs list the conditions for stable

Keyset pagination seeks to where you left off
Instead of a page number, the client sends back the last row it received, here its

Remember the last row, not the page number

tabs.label: ❌ Wrong
tabs.code:
-- Page N of "newest orders first"
SELECT Id, CreatedAt, Status, Total
FROM dbo.Orders
ORDER BY CreatedAt DESC, Id DESC
OFFSET @skip ROWS FETCH NEXT 20 ROWS ONLY;
-- Tested, last page: 1,000,000 rows scanned, 4,702 reads

tabs.label: ✅ Right
tabs.code:
-- Index: (CreatedAt, Id) INCLUDE (Status, Total)
-- The client sends back the last row's CreatedAt and Id
SELECT TOP (20) Id, CreatedAt, Status, Total
FROM dbo.Orders
WHERE CreatedAt < @lastCreatedAt
   OR (CreatedAt = @lastCreatedAt AND Id < @lastId)
ORDER BY CreatedAt DESC, Id DESC;
-- Tested, any page: Index Seek, 6 reads

content.text: Have the API return an opaque

token that encodes the last row's sort values, and accept it on the next call. Clients can't ask for page 50,000 by accident, and you can change the sort keys later without breaking them. For a "previous" link, reverse the comparisons and the sort, then reverse the 20 rows before returning them.
